lessons.title: Running a Fundraise: Pipeline, Outreach and Timelines

children.text: Most founders raise money the way an amateur sells: one conversation at a time, starting with whoever replies first, spread over five months, hoping somebody says yes before the cash runs out. Funds run a process. You should too. A fundraise is an enterprise sales cycle with one product, a small market of buyers and a hard deadline set by your bank balance. Run it as a process and you get competitive tension. Run it casually and you get a slow no.

body.text: Compress the process. The goal is not to meet the most investors, it is to get several credible investors to a decision in the same two weeks. Everything that makes fundraising work, including price, comes from that overlap.

children.text: The Funnel: Plan for the Conversion Rate, Not the Dream

Fundraising conversion rates are brutal and predictable. A well-matched list converts far better than a random one, but even a good process loses most of the pipeline at every stage. Plan the top of the funnel backwards from the number of term sheets you want.

body.caption: A realistic seed or Series A funnel

cells: Right stage, right cheque size, right sector, no portfolio conflict
A warm introduction and a one-liner they can repeat
Metrics that survive questioning, and a champion inside the fund
Clean data room, customer calls, references
An investment committee that says yes, and timing that lines up

body.title: Size the top of your funnel
body.prompt: A founder wants 2 term sheets. Historically, about 1 in every 30 well-matched investors approached produces one. How many investors should be on the target list?
body.explanation: 2 × 30 = 60. This is why founders who approach 12 investors and get nothing conclude the business is unfundable, when they have simply run too small a process. Note the phrase well-matched: 60 investors who fund your stage and sector, not 60 names scraped from a list.

body.text: Do not solve a small funnel by widening the criteria. Approaching funds that never write your cheque size wastes weeks and, worse, gets your deck circulating without conversations behind it. A tight list of 50 well-matched investors beats 200 names every time.

children.text: Tier the List Before You Send Anything

stats.label: Tier A
stats.context: Approach in week 2, once the pitch is sharp

stats.label: Tier B
stats.context: The core of the process, approached alongside Tier A

stats.label: Tier C
stats.context: Start here in week 1 to find the holes in your story

stats.label: Never
stats.context: They learn your numbers and have every reason to pass

children.text: The sequence matters. The first four pitches expose every weak answer in your deck, and you do not want to spend your best investor on that education. Start with Tier C, fix what broke, then open Tier A and B together so their processes run in parallel rather than one after another.

Every fund receives far more inbound than it can read. The filter is trust, so your job is to find a path. In order of strength: a founder the fund has already backed, an angel already on your cap table, another investor who passed but liked you, a lawyer or accountant who works with the fund, and finally a well-researched cold email. Accelerator and angel network alumni lists are the most underused source of warm paths in India.

body.title: The forwardable blurb: make it easy for the person introducing you

children.text: Never ask someone to "introduce me to a few investors". Send a short block of text they can forward without editing, so the favour takes them 20 seconds. Something like this:

Meera runs SampleTrail, which helps diagnostics labs in tier 2 cities track every sample from collection to report. 62 labs pay ₹4,000 a month, revenue has grown from ₹1.9 lakh to ₹4.8 lakh a month since March, and 88% of the labs that joined six months ago are still paying. She is raising ₹8 crore to expand across Maharashtra and Gujarat, and would value 30 minutes with you. Deck attached.

Three rules. Name the specific investor you want reached, so the connector is not left guessing. Give the introducer an easy way out, such as "no problem at all if you would rather not", because a reluctant introduction is worse than none. And always let the investor confirm interest before the introduction is made, which is the double opt-in convention most funds prefer.

body.label: Start the relationship before the raise
body.value: A short monthly update, six months early
body.context: Pick 15 investors you will eventually pitch, tell them you are not raising yet, and send a five-line monthly update with revenue, one win and one problem. When you do raise, you are not a stranger with a deck, you are a founder they have watched execute for six months.

events.title: Preparation
events.description: Build the deck, the model and the data room. Reconcile every number against your accounts. Build the target list of 50 to 60 investors and map an introduction path to each.

events.title: Practice round
events.description: Pitch Tier C. Note every question you answered badly, fix the deck, and tighten the story before it reaches anyone who matters.

events.title: First meetings
events.description: Open Tier A and Tier B together so their processes run in parallel. Aim for 20 to 25 first meetings inside a four-week window.

events.title: Second and partner meetings
events.description: Deeper dives on metrics, cohorts and the model. Identify who inside each fund is championing the deal, because that is what predicts a term sheet.

events.title: Diligence and term sheets
events.description: Data room access, customer and founder reference calls, investment committee meetings. Offers should land in the same fortnight, which is the entire point of compressing the process.

events.title: Negotiation, documents and closing
events.description: Negotiate the term sheet, then confirmatory diligence, definitive agreements, approvals and filings. This stage regularly takes longer than founders expect, as Lesson 4.3 shows.

body.title: When should you start?
body.prompt: A founder expects the raise to take 4 months from first pitch to money in the bank, wants 2 months of preparation before that, and insists on keeping at least 4 months of runway in reserve in case the round fails. What is the minimum runway, in months, she should have when she starts preparing?
body.explanation: 2 months preparing + 4 months raising + 4 months reserve = 10 months. Starting at 6 months of runway means negotiating from weakness, and starting at 3 means taking whatever terms arrive. The reserve is what lets you say no.

columns.label: The drip
points: Emails one investor a week as introductions come in
Each fund knows it is the only one deciding
By month four, the early investors ask why it is still open
One offer, take it or leave it

columns.label: The process
points: All outreach inside a three-week window
First meetings clustered, follow-ups scheduled tightly
Funds can sense parallel conversations without being told
Decisions land within the same fortnight
Two offers, and a real negotiation on price and terms

body.text: You do not need to bluff about other investors, and you should not. Simply saying "we are running a process this month and expect to decide by the end of it" is honest and creates the same urgency. Funds move fast when they believe a good deal may close without them.

markDefs.definition: The investor who sets the terms, usually takes the largest share of the round and does the deepest diligence. Other investors follow on those terms.

children.text: Most rounds stall for the same reason: every investor wants to follow and nobody wants to lead. A

sets the price and the terms, and the round fills once they commit. So identify which names on your list actually lead rounds of your size, and spend your best energy there. "We are interested once you have a lead" is not a commitment, it is a polite place in a queue.

body.title: Read the signal
body.question: Four investors respond in week 6 of a founder's process. Which response is worth the most?
options: "We love the space. Come back when you have a lead and we will take 10% of the round."
"Can you send the full financial model, cohort data and cap table? We want to bring this to our partner meeting next Tuesday."
"Great meeting. Let us stay in touch and track your progress over the next few quarters."
"Very impressive. We have just invested in an adjacent company, but do keep us posted."
body.explanation: A specific data request with a named internal meeting date is the clearest sign of a champion moving the deal forward. Waiting for a lead is a queue, tracking progress is a polite no for now, and an adjacent portfolio company usually means a conflict that will not clear.

body.title: Running the process like an operator
steps: One founder owns the raise, the other runs the company. A raise consumes a founder almost entirely.
Keep a simple tracker: investor, stage, last contact, next step, owner, date.
Hold a weekly review of the pipeline, exactly as you would for sales.
Send every follow-up within 24 hours, with the specific data asked for and nothing extra.
Send a short update to every live conversation each fortnight, especially good news.
Ask each investor at the first meeting how their process works and how long it takes.
When someone passes, ask what would have changed the answer, and write the reason down.
Never reveal who has passed, and never overstate other offers. Both come out later.

body.title: Five months of cash and three maybes
body.scenario: Ankit has been raising for three months for his Bengaluru B2B startup. He has approached 14 investors one at a time as introductions arrived. Three are still live: one wants to see two more months of data, one is waiting for a lead, and one has gone quiet after asking for cohort data six weeks ago. He has five months of runway, ₹1.6 crore of ARR growing 9% a month, and a co-founder running operations alone the whole time.
body.prompt: What should Ankit do over the next four weeks?
body.modelAnswer:
His problem is process, not business quality. 9% monthly growth on ₹1.6 crore of ARR is fundable.
Week 1: rebuild the funnel. Fourteen investors approached serially is roughly a fifth of a real process. Build a list of 45 to 55 well-matched investors, tier them, and map an introduction path to each, using his angels and any founders in those funds' portfolios.
Week 1 also: send the quiet investor the cohort data today with a one-line note saying the round is now on a defined timeline. Six weeks of silence after a data request usually means a soft pass, so treat it as information rather than hope.
Weeks 2 and 3: open 30 to 35 conversations inside a two-week window so decisions cluster. Tell everyone, truthfully, that he expects to close by a stated date.
Throughout: extend the runway. Trim discretionary spend so five months becomes seven, because every extra month of cash is negotiating leverage, and a failed raise with two months left is an existential event rather than a setback.
Also: the "waiting for a lead" investor is not a commitment, so stop counting it as one. The "two more months of data" investor is worth keeping warm with fortnightly updates, because he will have that data during the process.
And fix the division of labour. One founder should own the raise entirely while the other runs the company, which is what Ankit's co-founder has effectively been doing alone anyway.

body.title: The investor who unlocks the round
body.textWithBlank: The investor who sets the price and terms, takes the largest share and whose commitment lets the rest of the round fill is called the ___ investor.
body.explanation: Rounds stall when everyone wants to follow. Identify which funds actually lead at your cheque size and concentrate your effort there, because followers commit only after a lead has set the terms.

cards.definition: 50 to 60 investors matched on stage, cheque size and sector, with no portfolio conflict.
Splitting the list into practice conversations, core targets and top choices, then sequencing outreach accordingly.
A short pre-written paragraph an introducer can forward unedited, making the favour take seconds.
Checking that the investor wants the introduction before it is made, the convention most funds prefer.
The investor who sets terms and anchors the round, allowing followers to commit.
The person inside a fund who argues for your deal internally. No champion, no term sheet.
Running all conversations inside a short window so decisions land together and create real competition.

points: A fundraise is a sales process with a deadline set by your bank balance. Run it with a pipeline, stages and a weekly review.
Plan the funnel backwards: roughly 60 well-matched investors for 2 term sheets, not 12 conversations and hope.
Tier the list and pitch your practice tier first, so your best targets never hear the weak version of your story.
Warm introductions beat cold emails. Make them easy with a forwardable blurb and a double opt-in.
Start relationships six months early with short monthly updates, so you are a known quantity when you raise.
Compress everything into a three-week outreach window so decisions land in the same fortnight. That overlap is what creates negotiating power.
Find a lead investor. "Interested once you have a lead" is a queue, not a commitment.
Start preparing with around 10 months of runway, so you always keep a reserve that lets you walk away.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, legal or financial advice. Funnel conversion rates, timelines and list sizes are practical observations that vary by sector, stage and funding conditions, not benchmarks. Ankit, Meera and SampleTrail are illustrative. Speak to a qualified professional before making funding decisions for your company.
